lead: This unit shows how to turn the beam design of Units 2 and 3 into the design of slabs and staircases: flat plates that carry load by bending in one direction or two. After it you can pick the right slab type, take the right bending moment and shear, choose steel and check a slab for shear, deflection and cracking. You can also design a dog-legged staircase flight and read a flat slab panel through the direct design method.
about: Slabs are the largest concrete area in any building, so their design decides most of the steel and most of the cost. Chapter 4.1 takes a slab that bends in one direction only and designs a 1 m strip as a beam. Chapter 4.2 handles panels that bend both ways and the nine edge conditions of the code tables. Chapter 4.3 covers cantilever slabs, where the moment is hogging at the support, and continuous slabs designed from code moment coefficients. Chapter 4.4 applies the same strip design to an inclined dog-legged staircase. Chapter 4.5 introduces flat slabs, where the slab rests directly on columns and the moment splits into column and middle strips. Chapter 4.6 finds the collapse load of a slab from an assumed pattern of yield lines.

chapters.idea: A slab bending in one direction only is designed as a series of 1 m wide beams running along the short span.
chapters.depth: Take the slab as a 1 m wide strip and treat it as a simply supported or continuous beam. Cover the span/depth ratios used to guess the thickness, effective span, load build-up, factored load with 1.5 on dead plus live, Mu = wl²/8 and Vu = wl/2, steel from Mu/bd²fck, minimum steel, distribution steel at right angles, and the checks of shear, deflection and cracking. State clearly why ly/lx ≥ 2 makes the short span carry almost all the load. Some syllabi call it simply a slab spanning one way.

figure.title: Design of a 1 m strip of one-way slab

chapters.example: A simply supported one-way slab has a clear span of 3.0 m between 230 mm walls; the effective span is 3.0 m. Live load 3.0 kN/m², floor finish 1.0 kN/m², thickness 120 mm, M25 concrete, Fe415 steel, clear cover 20 mm. Find the factored moment and the main and distribution steel.
chapters.trap: Writing the load as a total in kN instead of kN/m on a 1 m strip, and using the full slab width in Mu/bd². Also forgetting distribution steel and using the wrong cover when finding d.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (partial safety factors, stress block) and Unit 2 (singly reinforced flexure, Mu/bd²fck).
chapters.leave: Beam shear reinforcement design (Unit 3) and full deflection theory (Unit 2); here only the slab checks are applied.

chapters.idea: When the long span is less than twice the short span, load travels both ways and the code gives separate coefficients for each direction and each edge condition.
chapters.depth: Define lx, ly and why ly/lx ≤ 2 makes the panel two-way. Give the Rankine–Grashoff split of load in the two directions as the idea behind the coefficients, then the IS 456 Table 26 coefficients αx and αy for negative and positive moments over the nine boundary cases, including the interior panel. Show Mx = αx w lx² and My = αy w ly², steel in both directions with the longer-span steel placed above the shorter-span steel, corner torsion reinforcement, and the checks. Use the names one short edge continuous, two adjacent edges discontinuous, and so on, as some syllabi word them.
chapters.example: A 140 mm thick slab covers an effective panel of 4.0 m × 5.0 m. Two adjacent edges are discontinuous and the other two are continuous over beams. Live load 4.0 kN/m², floor finish 1.0 kN/m², M25 concrete, Fe415 steel, cover 20 mm. Find the factored moments in both directions and the steel.
chapters.trap: Using clear spans instead of effective spans to get ly/lx, reading the coefficient row for the wrong edge case, and swapping αx and αy so the long span gets the short-span moment.
chapters.leave: Yield line collapse of the same panel (Chapter 4.6) and flat slab strip division (Chapter 4.5).

chapters.idea: A cantilever slab carries hogging moment at its support, while a continuous slab is designed from code coefficients that already allow for pattern loading.
chapters.depth: For the cantilever: load per metre, M = wl²/2 with l measured to the face of the support, steel at the top anchored into the back span, check of deflection at the tip and of development length at the support. For continuous slabs: the IS 456 coefficient tables for negative and positive moments under UDL, the conditions that allow their use (three or more equal spans, uniform load, span within 15 percent of the longest), the moment envelope, curtailment of top steel, and why pattern loading puts the largest sagging moment in alternate spans.
chapters.example: A cantilever slab projects 1.5 m clear from a beam face. Live load 3.0 kN/m², floor finish 1.0 kN/m², thickness 150 mm, M25 concrete, Fe415 steel, cover 20 mm. Find the hogging moment at the support and the main steel. Then state how a three-span continuous slab of 3.0 m each, carrying the same loads, is designed with the coefficient method.
chapters.trap: Measuring the cantilever span to the centre of the support instead of the face, and placing the main steel at the bottom of a cantilever. In continuous slabs, using coefficients outside the conditions the code allows.
chapters.leave: Moment distribution and stiffness analysis of continuous beams to a structural analysis course; here only the code coefficients are used.

chapters.idea: A dog-legged staircase flight is a sloping one-way slab, the waist slab, designed as an inclined beam between landings.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the other staircase types in detail. Cover riser and tread, going, floor-to-floor height, the two flights with a half landing, effective span of a flight, load on the waist slab with the slope factor, the landing slab designed as a short span, and the same flexure, shear and deflection checks as a slab. Describe the other types in one or two lines each: open well, straight flight, and stringer beam stairs. Do not derive the slope factor; just use it.
chapters.example: Design the waist slab of a dog-legged staircase. Floor-to-floor height 3.0 m, riser 150 mm, tread 300 mm, so 10 risers per flight. Waist slab 150 mm thick, landing 1.2 m wide, effective span of each flight 3.3 m, live load 3.0 kN/m², floor finish 1.0 kN/m², M25 concrete, Fe415 steel, cover 20 mm.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the slope factor, so the waist slab weight is taken on the inclined length while the moment is taken on the horizontal span. Also mixing load per metre of horizontal run with load per metre of sloping length.
chapters.leave: Lateral stability of the stair well and landing beam design to the beam units; only the flight and landing slab are designed here.

chapters.idea: A flat slab carries load straight to columns, and the total static moment of a panel is split into negative and positive parts and then into column and middle strips.
chapters.depth: Introduction only: no beams, slab on columns, capitals and drops, and why the slab must resist punching shear at the column. Cover the direct design method for a panel of equal spans: total static moment M0 = w l2 ln²/8 with ln the clear span between column faces, the split into 65 percent negative and 35 percent positive, the column strip taking most of the negative moment and the middle strip most of the positive, and the design moment per metre for each strip. Mention punching shear and the check at the column face in words; do not design punching reinforcement.

figure.title: Direct design method for one flat slab panel

chapters.example: A flat slab floor has panels of 6.0 m × 6.0 m centre to centre on 400 mm square columns. Slab thickness 180 mm, live load 4.0 kN/m², floor finish 1.0 kN/m², M25 concrete, Fe415 steel. Using the direct design method, find the total static moment M0, split it into negative and positive moments, and give the design moment per metre in the column strip and the middle strip.
chapters.trap: Using the centre-to-centre span instead of the clear span ln in M0, and dividing a strip moment by the wrong width, so the student reports a per-panel moment as a per-metre moment.
chapters.leave: Punching shear reinforcement, the equivalent frame method and design of columns and footings to Unit 5 and to a later course.

chapters.idea: Yield line theory assumes a pattern of straight hinge lines, equates the work of the load to the work absorbed at those lines, and gives a collapse load that is never lower than the true one.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic. Define the plastic moment of resistance Mp per metre, the yield line, and the virtual displacement. Show the two sides of virtual work: external work, load times the volume swept, and internal work, Mp times yield line length times the relative rotation across the line. Solve the square simply supported slab to get wu = 24 Mp/L², mention the upper bound nature, and that the lowest load from all admissible patterns governs. No derivation of other patterns beyond one rectangular or one with a free edge, in words.

figure.title: Virtual work on a yield line pattern

chapters.example: A square slab 4.0 m × 4.0 m is simply supported on all four edges and reinforced with 10 mm bars at 150 mm centres both ways at an effective depth of 100 mm. M25 concrete, Fe415 steel. Find Mp per metre width and use yield line theory to find the uniform collapse load wu.
chapters.trap: Using the rotation of each plate about its own support edge rather than the relative rotation across the yield line, which gives half the true internal work. Also treating the lowest wu as wrong because it is an upper bound.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (moment of resistance of a section) and Chapter 4.2.
chapters.leave: Plastic analysis of beams and frames to a structural analysis course; serviceability checks of slabs to Chapters 4.1 to 4.3.
